messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not change the change in BDI-II depressive symptom score compared with placebo in all subjects.
Sentence: "At the end of the study, there were no significant differences in Δ BDI-II score (score at the end of the study minus score at baseline), regardless of analysing all subjects, subjects with or without psycopharmaca, or if performing subgroup analyses based on baseline and final serum 25(OH)D levels combined with categories of baseline BDI-II scores >4 or >13."
Measured as: Δ BDI-II score (Beck Depression Inventory-II)
Population: 408 adults (mean age ~52 years) randomised to vitamin D or placebo; few clinically depressed
Intervention: Vitamin D 100,000 IU bolus followed by 20,000 IU per week for 4 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 408
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Depression scores on the HADs improved significantly more with vitamin D3 than with placebo in IBS-D patients.
Sentence: "Symptoms severity, QoL, HADs-depression, and VSI score improved significantly in the vitamin D group as compared to the placebo group (P-values: <0.001, 0.049, 0.023, and 0.008; respectively)."
Measured as: HADs-depression score
Population: Adults aged 18-65 with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome
Intervention: Vitamin D3 50,000 IU/week for 9 weeks
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 74
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are placebo-controlled RCTs on depressive symptoms, but Study A enrolled mostly non-depressed general adults with low vitamin D and used BDI-II, while Study B enrolled IBS-D patients, used HADs-depression, and gave a shorter, differently dosed course.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["intervention","outcome_measure"],"detail":"population: mostly non-depressed adults with low 25(OH)D (n=408) vs IBS-D patients (n=74); 4 months at 20,000 IU/week vs 9 weeks at 50,000 IU/week"}
